terms.meaning: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, which requires clear consent for specific uses of personal data.
A named reason a service uses personal data, such as AI chat or summaries.
A value added to a web address after a question mark, such as the purpose name in the status route.
A network address that identifies the device making a request.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and setup
sections.what: Brings in the NestJS tools for routes, query and header reading, the documentation tags, the signed-in user helper, the consent service and the request shapes.
sections.why: Likely reason: each import supports the routes below.

sections.name: ConsentController
sections.title: Consent routes
sections.what: Defines routes to grant consent, revoke consent, list all consents for the user, and check one purpose. Grant and revoke also record the browser type and network address.
sections.why: Likely reason: recording these details gives a record of when and how consent was given or withdrawn.
sections.watch_out: The status route accepts any purpose text, so an unknown purpose returns false and looks the same as a refused one.

summary: Gives the signed-in user routes to grant, withdraw, list and check their data-use consents.
purpose: Lets a user manage their own consents and lets other parts of the app check whether a specific use is allowed.
why: Likely reason: DPDP requires that users agree to specific uses of their data and can withdraw that agreement, and the routes record proof of each choice.
how: 1. Granting a consent passes the purpose and the browser and network details to the service. 2. Revoking does the same for withdrawal. 3. Listing returns all of the user's consent records. 4. The status route takes a purpose name and returns whether it is currently granted.
inputs: The signed-in user id, the purpose and related details in the request body, the browser type header, the network address, and the purpose name in the status query.
outputs: Consent records, or an object showing the purpose and whether it is granted.
risks: The status route accepts any text as the purpose and returns false for unknown names, so a typo looks like a refused consent. Ownership is handled by the service, which is not visible here.
debug: Check the consent record in the database. Confirm the browser and network details are stored. A 400 response points to the request body or the purpose name.
